lessons.title: Energy Systems: Metabolizable Energy (ME) and Net Energy (NE)
lessons.body: Energy is the most expensive part of any poultry feed, so you must get it right. In Africa, maize is the main energy source, but its quality varies. Metabolizable Energy (ME) is the energy birds can actually use after digestion and losses in urine and gases. Net Energy (NE) goes further, subtracting the energy lost as heat. For practical feed formulation, we use ME because tables are widely available. For broilers, starter feed needs 3000-3100 kcal ME/kg, grower 3100-3200, and finisher 3200-3300. Layers need about 2700-2800 kcal ME/kg. If you use cassava instead of maize, remember cassava has lower ME (about 2800 kcal/kg) and needs added oil or fat to reach target. A simple method: use a feed formulation software like Feedsoft or Excel. Enter ingredient ME values from NRC (1994) or your local feed lab. For example, maize ME = 3350 kcal/kg, soybean meal = 2440 kcal/kg, fishmeal = 2900 kcal/kg. To increase energy, add 1-2% vegetable oil (palm oil or sunflower oil), which gives about 9000 kcal/kg. But too much oil makes feed rancid and sticky. In hot African climates, birds eat less, so you must increase nutrient density. If birds eat 100g/day instead of 120g, you need 20% more energy per kg. Always check feed intake. A quick test: if broilers are not reaching target weight by day 21 (should be around 800-900g), energy may be low. Also, ME is not enough; consider NE for precision, but most African feed mills stick to ME. Remember, energy interacts with protein: too much energy and not enough protein gives fat birds; too little energy and birds eat more, wasting protein. Balance is key. Use local ingredients: maize, millet, sorghum, cassava chips, and by-products like wheat bran (lower ME, about 1300 kcal/kg). Always test your maize for moisture and aflatoxin. Aflatoxin reduces energy use and harms birds. So, buy good maize, dry it to below 14% moisture, and store in dry place. Thatâs how you control energy cost and bird performance.

lessons.title: Crude Protein vs. Amino Acid Requirements
lessons.body: Crude protein (CP) is a rough measure. It counts all nitrogen, but birds need specific amino acids (AA) to build muscle and eggs. Think of CP as the total bricks, but AA are the different shapes you need. The most critical AA are lysine, methionine, threonine, and tryptophan. For broilers, starter needs 22-23% CP, but more importantly, 1.2% lysine and 0.5% methionine. Layers need 16-18% CP, with 0.8% lysine and 0.35% methionine. In Africa, soybean meal is the gold standard for AA, but itâs expensive. You can use alternatives: groundnut cake (lower lysine), sunflower cake (low lysine, high fibre), fishmeal (excellent but costly), and cottonseed cake (use with caution, gossypol). To meet AA, you must combine ingredients. For example, maize is low in lysine, so you add soybean meal. If you use 60% maize and 25% soybean meal, you get about 18% CP and 0.9% lysine. For layers, add 0.1% synthetic methionine and 0.05% lysine. Synthetic AA are cheap and effective. Always use a least-cost formulation software. If you donât have one, use the Pearson Square method for two ingredients, but it only balances CP, not AA. So, you need AA tables. The NRC (1994) gives AA requirements. For example, broiler 0-3 weeks: lysine 1.10%, methionine 0.50%, methionine+cysteine 0.90%, threonine 0.80%, tryptophan 0.20%. For layers: lysine 0.80%, methionine 0.35%, methionine+cysteine 0.60%. In hot weather, birds eat less, so increase AA density by 5-10%. Also, watch for anti-nutritional factors: raw soybeans have trypsin inhibitors that reduce protein digestibility. Always toast or buy properly processed soybean meal. In Africa, many farmers use fishmeal from local markets; test for salt content (should be <3%) and rancidity. A practical tip: if your birds have poor feathering or cannibalism, it may be methionine deficiency. Add 0.05% methionine. For eggs, if egg size is small, increase methionine and lysine. Remember, CP is not enough; you must balance AA. Thatâs how you save money and get results.

lessons.title: Macro and Micro Minerals in Poultry Diets
lessons.body: Minerals are needed in small amounts but are critical. Macro minerals: calcium, phosphorus, sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium. Micro minerals: zinc, manganese, iron, copper, iodine, selenium. In Africa, the biggest problems are calcium and phosphorus. For layers, calcium is key for eggshells. A layer needs 3.5-4.0% calcium. Use limestone or oyster shell. But particle size matters: give 50% as fine powder and 50% as small stones (2-3mm) for slow release. For broilers, calcium needs are lower: starter 1.0%, finisher 0.9%. Phosphorus: available phosphorus (not total) is what matters. Broilers need 0.45% available P, layers 0.35%. Most plant phosphorus is bound as phytate, so you must add phytase enzyme (500 FTU/kg) to release it. Without phytase, add dicalcium phosphate (DCP) or bone meal. But DCP is expensive. In Africa, many use rock phosphate, but it may have fluoride â avoid. Sodium and chloride: add 0.2-0.3% salt. Too much salt causes wet litter. Potassium: usually enough in feed. Micro minerals: zinc (80-100 ppm), manganese (80-100 ppm), iron (50-80 ppm), copper (8-10 ppm), iodine (0.5-1 ppm), selenium (0.2-0.3 ppm). You can buy a commercial mineral premix. If not, use local sources: zinc sulphate, manganese sulphate. But be careful with copper â too much is toxic. In some African countries, soil is selenium-deficient, so add selenium. Also, mycotoxins bind minerals, so use toxin binders. A practical method: mix your own premix using a carrier like maize bran. For 100 kg feed, add: 1 kg limestone, 0.5 kg DCP, 0.3 kg salt, 0.1 kg mineral premix. But always check your local ingredient mineral content. For example, fishmeal has high calcium and phosphorus. If you use 5% fishmeal, reduce DCP. Also, excess calcium interferes with phosphorus and zinc absorption. So balance. Test your feed occasionally at a lab. If eggshells are thin or broken, increase calcium. If birds have leg problems, check phosphorus and vitamin D3. Remember, minerals are cheap but mistakes are costly.

lessons.title: Vitamin Requirements and Supplementation
lessons.body: Vitamins are needed in tiny amounts but control many body functions. There are fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble vitamins (B-complex, C). In African poultry, deficiencies are common because feed ingredients lose vitamins during storage. For example, maize stored for 6 months loses vitamin E. So, you must add a vitamin premix. For broilers, a standard premix provides per kg feed: vitamin A 10,000-15,000 IU, D3 2,000-3,000 IU, E 30-50 IU, K 2-3 mg, B1 2-3 mg, B2 6-8 mg, B6 3-5 mg, B12 0.01-0.02 mg, niacin 30-50 mg, pantothenic acid 10-15 mg, folic acid 0.5-1 mg, biotin 0.1-0.2 mg. For layers, similar but often higher vitamin D3 (3,000-4,000 IU) for eggshell quality. In hot climates, add vitamin C (100-200 mg/kg) to reduce heat stress. You can buy commercial premixes from companies like DSM, BASF, or local feed stores. If you canât afford premix, use fresh green feed like moringa, amaranth, or sweet potato leaves â but these are not enough for high-producing birds. A practical approach: buy a good quality premix and store it in a cool, dark place. Never use expired premix. Mix it into feed within 3 months. Also, watch for interactions: excess vitamin A interferes with D. Excess D is toxic. In Africa, many farmers use liver or fish oil as vitamin source, but these are inconsistent. For example, cod liver oil has A and D, but it can go rancid. Better to use synthetic vitamins. For small-scale farmers, you can make a simple premix: for 100 kg feed, add 100 g of commercial vitamin premix. If you see symptoms like curled toe paralysis (riboflavin deficiency), add extra B2. If birds have poor growth and rough feathers, check vitamin A. For layers, if egg production drops and shells are thin, increase vitamin D3. Remember, vitamins are destroyed by heat, light, and moisture. So, store feed in a dry place and use within 4 weeks. Also, moldy feed destroys vitamins. Always use mold inhibitors like propionic acid. A good practice: include 1-2% vegetable oil to help absorb fat-soluble vitamins. In summary, vitamins are cheap insurance â donât skip them.

lessons.title: Water Quality and Its Impact on Nutrition
lessons.body: Water is the most important nutrient. Birds drink 1.5-2 times their feed intake. If water is bad, feed is wasted. In Africa, water sources often have high salts, bacteria, or algae. You must test water at least once a year. Key parameters: pH (6.5-8.5), total dissolved solids (TDS) <1000 ppm, hardness, nitrate <50 ppm, sulfate <250 ppm, chloride <250 ppm, iron <0.3 ppm, manganese <0.05 ppm. High TDS (e.g., 2000 ppm) causes wet litter and poor growth. High sulfate (>500 ppm) causes diarrhea. High iron (>5 ppm) supports bacterial growth and clogs drinkers. High nitrate (>100 ppm) reduces oxygen in blood. In many African farms, borehole water has high iron and manganese. You can treat with chlorination (2-5 ppm chlorine) or use filters. But chlorine kills vitamins in water if you add vitamins via water. So, if you give vitamins in water, do it 2 hours after chlorination or use hydrogen peroxide. Also, water pH affects vaccine and drug efficacy. For example, pH >8 reduces amprolium. A practical method: test water with a simple kit from a pharmacy or agricultural store. If TDS is high, use reverse osmosis or mix with rainwater. Rainwater is soft but can be contaminated. Always cover tanks. Clean drinkers daily with a brush and disinfect weekly. In hot weather, birds drink more, so water quality becomes even more critical. If birds refuse water, check for off-flavors from algae or bacteria. Add 0.5% vinegar (acetic acid) to lower pH and control algae. But donât overdo it. Also, water temperature: birds prefer 10-20Â°C. In hot climates, water in black tanks can reach 40Â°C, reducing intake. So, bury pipes or use white tanks. A good rule: if you wouldnât drink it, donât give it to your birds. Poor water quality reduces feed conversion, increases disease, and costs you money. So, invest in water testing and treatment. Itâs cheaper than medication.

lessons.title: Using NRC and Commercial Feeding Standards
lessons.body: Feeding standards are tables that tell you how much of each nutrient to include in feed for different bird ages and types. The most common are NRC (National Research Council) and commercial company standards (e.g., Cobb, Ross, Hy-Line). NRC (1994) is the classic reference, but itâs old. Modern genetics have changed requirements. For example, NRC broiler 0-3 weeks: 3200 kcal ME/kg, 23% CP, 1.10% lysine. But Cobb 500 (2022) recommends 3000 kcal ME/kg, 22% CP, 1.20% lysine. So, commercial standards are more up-to-date. In Africa, you can get these manuals from breed company websites or local distributors. Use them as a starting point. But you must adjust for local conditions: heat stress, disease pressure, ingredient quality. For example, in hot climates, reduce CP by 1-2% and increase synthetic amino acids to lower heat production. Also, if your maize is low in energy (e.g., 3200 kcal/kg instead of 3350), you need to add oil. A practical method: take the commercial standard, then use a feed formulation software to match it with your available ingredients. If you donât have software, use the Pearson Square for energy and protein, then add a premix to cover vitamins and minerals. But remember, Pearson Square only balances two nutrients. For AA, you need to check with tables. Many African feed mills use NRC because itâs free, but they tweak it. For example, for layers, NRC says 16% CP, 0.8% lysine, but Hy-Line W-36 recommends 16.5% CP, 0.85% lysine for peak production. So, always use the breedâs recommendation. Also, consider feed form: mash, crumble, or pellet. Pelleting improves feed efficiency by 5-10%, so you can reduce nutrient density slightly. But pelleting is expensive. For small-scale farmers, mash is fine. Another tool: use the âideal proteinâ concept, where you balance all AA relative to lysine. For broilers, ideal ratio: lysine 100, methionine 38, methionine+cysteine 72, threonine 65, tryptophan 17. For layers: lysine 100, methionine 45, methionine+cysteine 80, threonine 70, tryptophan 20. This helps you use synthetic AA efficiently. Finally, always keep records: feed intake, weight gain, egg production. Compare with standards. If birds are below target, adjust. Thatâs how you learn. Donât just copy a table â adapt it to your farm.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Nutrient Requirements and Feeding Standards for Broilers and Layers

In African poultry production, feed represents 65â75% of total production cost. A single percentage point of wasted energy or an avoidable amino acid deficiency can erase the entire margin on a batch of 500 broilers. This lesson gives you a practical reference framework for applying energy, protein, mineral, vitamin and water standards using NRC and commercial specifications, tuned to the realities of small and medium-scale African farms.

Business-first principle: you do not formulate to impress a laboratory. You formulate to hit a target weight, egg number, or feed conversion ratio at the lowest cost per kilogram of live weight or per egg. Every number below should be read as a cost lever, not an academic constant.

1. Energy Systems: ME and NE in Practice

Metabolizable Energy (ME) is the standard for poultry in Africa because it is measurable and widely published. Net Energy (NE) is more accurate because it accounts for heat increment and the efficiency of use of different nutrients, but NE tables for local ingredients are scarce. Practical approach: formulate on ME, but adjust for high-fibre, high-protein ingredients that inflate heat increment â a diet heavy in cottonseed cake or palm kernel cake will underperform its ME value in hot African climates.

2. Crude Protein vs Amino Acid Requirements

Crude protein (CP) is a crude proxy. What the bird actually needs is a balanced profile of essential amino acids (EAAs), especially lysine, methionine, threonine and tryptophan. In African markets, methionine and lysine are often imported and expensive, so over-formulating CP wastes money twice: you buy protein the bird cannot use, and you pay for the synthetic amino acids anyway to correct the balance.

Business rule: for broilers, target digestible lysine first, then methionine + cysteine, then threonine. For layers, methionine is the first limiting amino acid for egg mass. Use "ideal protein" ratios relative to lysine (e.g., methionine 50%, threonine 67%, tryptophan 18% of lysine) to reduce CP by 1â2 percentage points without performance loss, cutting soybean meal costs.

3. Macro and Micro Minerals

Calcium and available phosphorus dominate mineral cost and bird health. In Africa, limestone and bone meal are locally available, but quality varies. Dicalcium phosphate is often imported. Non-phytate phosphorus (available P) is the practical metric, not total P. Phytase enzymes are cost-effective: adding 500â1000 FTU/kg can release 0.08â0.12% available P, reducing inorganic phosphate inclusion.

Micro minerals (zinc, copper, iron, manganese, selenium, iodine) are required in small amounts but deficiencies cause silent profit leaks: poor shell quality, footpad lesions, reduced immunity. Organic trace minerals (chelates) improve absorption under disease challenge but cost more; use them strategically in breeder and layer diets.

4. Vitamins and Supplementation

Vitamin premixes are the most common hidden cost variable. In hot, humid African conditions, vitamin potency degrades faster in stored feed. Vitamin A, D3, E and K are critical; B-complex vitamins affect hatchability and growth. Over-supplementation is common and wasteful; under-supplementation causes deficiency diseases that cost more than the premix.

Practical approach: use a commercial premix matched to the species and production stage, store feed < 4 weeks, and avoid mixing premixes into hot mash. In heat stress, increase vitamin C and E inclusion by 20â30%.

5. Water Quality and Nutrition

Water is the most neglected nutrient. A bird drinks roughly twice its feed intake. If water contains high salts, nitrates, or microbial load, feed conversion worsens even with a perfectly formulated diet. In many African farms, borehole water has elevated total dissolved solids (TDS), sulphates, or iron, which reduce water intake and nutrient absorption.

Test water at least twice a year. Target: TDS < 1000 ppm, nitrate < 50 ppm, pH 6.5â8.0, total bacterial count low. If water is marginal, consider acidifiers, chlorine, or alternative sources. Water quality directly determines whether your feed investment converts to meat or eggs.

6. Using NRC and Commercial Feeding Standards

NRC (1994) remains the global reference but is based on temperate conditions and older genetics. Modern commercial standards (e.g., Aviagen Ross 308, Hy-Line, Cobb) are more current and breed-specific. In Africa, use commercial standards as the baseline, then adjust for:

  • Local ingredient nutrient variability (test your maize, soybean meal, fishmeal)
  • Heat stress (reduce energy density slightly, increase amino acids and electrolytes)
  • Disease pressure (increase vitamins and trace minerals)
  • Market weight targets and egg size premiums

â  SAFETY WARNING â Selenium and Vitamin D Toxicity

Exceeding 0.5 mg/kg selenium or 5,000 IU/kg vitamin D3 in poultry feed can cause acute toxicity, reduced feed intake, kidney damage, and mortality. Never double-dose a premix to "catch up" after a deficiency. Always weigh premixes accurately, mix thoroughly, and store away from direct sunlight. In Africa, where premix scoops are often used instead of scales, invest in a 0.1 g precision scale â it costs less than one lost batch.

Quick Reference Checklist (6â8 Points)

  1. Test your ingredients: Maize, soybean meal and fishmeal vary widely in Africa. A single crude protein test (Kjeldahl or NIR) can save a whole batch.
  2. Formulate on digestible amino acids, not crude protein: Use lysine as the reference and balance methionine, threonine and tryptophan.
  3. Use phytase: 500â1000 FTU/kg releases 0.08â0.12% available P, reducing imported phosphate costs.
  4. Match energy to climate: In heat stress, reduce ME slightly and increase amino acid density and electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride).
  5. Store feed < 4 weeks: Vitamin potency and fat quality degrade fast in hot, humid conditions.
  6. Test water twice a year: TDS < 1000 ppm, nitrate < 50 ppm, pH 6.5â8.0. Water quality is a feed cost multiplier.
  7. Use commercial breed standards, not just NRC: Ross, Cobb and Hy-Line guides are updated for modern genetics and are free online.
  8. Calculate cost per kg live weight or per egg, not per tonne of feed: The cheapest feed per tonne is often the most expensive per kilogram of output.

Further Reading (Free Official Links)

  • NRC (1994) Nutrient Requirements of Poultry, 9th Revised Edition â National Academies Press (free read online)
  • Aviagen Ross 308 Broiler Nutrition Specifications â free download
  • Hy-Line International Management Guides (Brown, W-36, etc.) â free download
  • FAO Poultry Production and Products â technical resources and manuals
  • Cobb-Vantress Resource Center â broiler nutrition and management guides

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Broiler and Layer Feed Formulation. Always validate formulations with a qualified nutritionist and local ingredient analyses before large-scale mixing.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between Metabolizable Energy (ME) and Net Energy (NE)?
options: A) ME includes energy lost in urine and gases, NE does not
B) NE is always higher than ME
C) ME is only for layers, NE for broilers
D) NE is easier to measure
quiz.explanation: ME subtracts energy lost in urine and gases, while NE further subtracts heat loss.

quiz.q: For a broiler starter diet, what is the recommended ME range?
quiz.explanation: Broiler starter typically requires 3000-3100 kcal ME/kg for optimal growth.

quiz.q: Which ingredient is commonly used in Africa to increase energy density of poultry feed?
quiz.explanation: Vegetable oils like palm oil provide about 9000 kcal/kg and are used to boost energy.

quiz.q: Why is cassava a challenging energy source in poultry feed?
options: B) It has low ME and needs added fat
C) It is toxic to birds
quiz.explanation: Cassava has lower ME (about 2800 kcal/kg) than maize and requires oil supplementation.

quiz.q: In hot African climates, why should you increase nutrient density?
quiz.explanation: Heat stress reduces feed intake, so each kg of feed must contain more nutrients.

quiz.q: What is the most critical amino acid for broiler muscle development?
quiz.explanation: Lysine is the first limiting amino acid for muscle growth in broilers.

quiz.q: Which ingredient is a good source of lysine but is expensive?
quiz.explanation: Soybean meal is rich in lysine and other amino acids but costly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended methionine level for broiler starter?
quiz.explanation: Broiler starter requires about 0.50% methionine for optimal growth.

quiz.q: What is a common symptom of methionine deficiency in poultry?
quiz.explanation: Methionine deficiency leads to poor feathering and cannibalism due to stress.

quiz.q: Which method can balance crude protein but not amino acids?
quiz.explanation: Pearson Square only balances two nutrients like CP and energy, not individual amino acids.

quiz.q: What is the recommended calcium level for laying hens?
quiz.explanation: Layers need 3.5-4.0% calcium for strong eggshells.

quiz.q: Why is particle size of calcium important for layers?
options: B) Large particles release calcium slowly
quiz.explanation: Large calcium particles (2-3mm) stay in the gut longer, providing calcium for shell formation at night.

quiz.q: What enzyme helps release phytate-bound phosphorus?
quiz.explanation: Phytase breaks down phytate, making phosphorus available to the bird.

quiz.q: Which mineral is important for eggshell formation?
quiz.explanation: Calcium is the primary mineral in eggshells.

quiz.q: What is a sign of calcium deficiency in layers?
quiz.explanation: Calcium deficiency leads to thin or soft eggshells.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is critical for calcium absorption and eggshell quality?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin D3 regulates calcium and phosphorus metabolism for shell formation.

quiz.q: What is a common symptom of riboflavin (B2) deficiency?
quiz.explanation: Riboflavin deficiency causes curled toe paralysis in chicks.

quiz.q: Why should you add vitamin C to poultry feed in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin C helps birds cope with heat stress by reducing oxidative damage.

quiz.q: How should vitamin premix be stored?
options: A) In a warm, bright place
B) In a cool, dark, dry place
quiz.explanation: Vitamins degrade with heat, light, and moisture, so cool, dark, dry storage is essential.

quiz.q: What is the effect of excess vitamin A on vitamin D?
options: B) It interferes with D utilization
quiz.explanation: Excess vitamin A antagonizes vitamin D, leading to poor bone and shell quality.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pH range for poultry drinking water?
quiz.explanation: Poultry water should be near neutral, between pH 6.5 and 8.5.

quiz.q: What problem does high iron in water cause?
options: B) Clogged drinkers and bacterial growth
quiz.explanation: High iron supports bacteria and forms deposits that clog drinkers.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid chlorinating water when adding vitamins?
options: B) Chlorine makes water taste bad
D) Chlorine is toxic to birds
quiz.explanation: Chlorine destroys vitamins, especially A and E, so add vitamins after chlorine dissipates.

quiz.q: What is a simple treatment to control algae in water tanks?
quiz.explanation: Vinegar lowers pH and inhibits algae growth.

quiz.q: What is the recommended TDS level for poultry water?
quiz.explanation: Total dissolved solids should be below 1000 ppm for good poultry performance.

quiz.q: Which organization publishes widely used poultry nutrient requirement tables?
quiz.explanation: The National Research Council (NRC) publishes standard nutrient requirement tables.

quiz.q: Why might you adjust NRC standards for modern broilers?
options: B) Modern genetics have different requirements
C) NRC is for layers only
D) NRC is outdated and not used
quiz.explanation: Modern broiler strains have higher growth rates and require updated nutrient levels.

quiz.q: What is the ideal protein concept?
options: A) Balancing all amino acids relative to lysine
quiz.explanation: Ideal protein balances amino acids as a ratio to lysine for optimal utilization.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of pelleting feed?
quiz.explanation: Pelleting improves feed conversion and reduces waste.

quiz.q: What should you do if your birds are not meeting target weight?
options: B) Adjust feed formulation based on records
quiz.explanation: Record keeping and comparing with standards helps identify needed adjustments.
